french-saint-christophe.t: France's first lasting colony in the Caribbean, on Saint Kitts, base for the settlement of Guadeloupe and Martinique.
french-saint-christophe.o: The Norman captain [[e:pierre-belain-desnambuc|Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc]] landed on [[e:saint-kitts|Saint Christopher]] in 1625 and, with the backing of [[e:cardinal-richelieu|Cardinal Richelieu's]] [[e:compagnie-de-saint-christophe|Compagnie de Saint-Christophe]], founded a French colony. In 1627 the French and English partitioned the island, the French taking the two ends, including [[e:basseterre|Basseterre]].
french-saint-christophe.r: French Saint-Christophe grew tobacco and later [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], worked by indentured servants and enslaved Africans. From here [[e:pierre-belain-desnambuc|d'Esnambuc]] launched the settlement of [[s:colony-of-martinique|Martinique]] in 1635. [[e:phillippe-de-longvilliers-de-poincy|Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy]], governor-general of the [[e:french-antilles|French Antilles]] from 1639, ruled from a grand château on the island and bought it for the [[e:knights-hospitaller|Knights of Malta]] in 1651.
french-saint-christophe.e: The French and English repeatedly expelled each other during the wars of the late 17th century. By the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 [[e:france|France]] ceded its share to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], merging it into the [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Colony of Saint Christopher]].

free-imperial-city-of-obernai.t: Alsatian wine town below Mont Sainte-Odile, birthplace of Alsace's patron saint and a member of the Decapolis league of imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.o: Obernai lies at the foot of [[e:mont-sainte-odile|Mont Sainte-Odile]] and is held to be the birthplace of [[e:saint-odile|Saint Odile]], patron saint of [[e:alsace|Alsace]]. A [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] town, it was recognised as an imperial city in the 1280s, around 1283, and in 1354 it joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the league of ten Alsatian imperial cities.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ruled this prosperous small town, which lived from wine, grain and crafts. Its market square, town hall and corn hall reflect late medieval and [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] prosperity. Obernai remained Catholic during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. Like the other [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] cities, it suffered heavily during [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-obernai.e: After the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] gave [[e:france|France]] rights in [[e:alsace|Alsace]], French troops occupied the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], and the [[e:treaties-of-nijmegen|Treaty of Nijmegen]] in 1679 confirmed French rule. Obernai is now a town in Alsace, France.

free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.t: A Neckar wine and trading city whose imperial charter of 1371 made it a self-governing republic of burghers until 1802.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.o: Heilbronn grew around a royal estate at a [[e:neckar|Neckar]] crossing, first mentioned in 741. The town received a charter from Rudolf I in 1281, and in 1371 Charles IV granted it a constitution that confirmed its status as a free imperial city and gave power to a council drawn from patricians and guildsmen.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.r: Heilbronn lived from [[e:neckar|Neckar]] shipping, which it controlled through its weir, and from vineyards. The city accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1528 under the preacher [[e:johann-lachmann|Johann Lachmann]]. The knight [[e:gotz-von-berlichingen|Götz von Berlichingen]] was held prisoner in its tower in 1519, and in 1633 [[e:sweden|Sweden]] and the Protestant estates concluded the [[e:heilbronn-league|Heilbronn League]] there.
free-imperial-city-of-heilbronn.e: Heilbronn was annexed by Württemberg in 1802 and became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. Heavily bombed in December 1944, it was rebuilt and is now an industrial and wine centre in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]].

free-state-of-waldeck.t: Small Hessian republic, successor of the Principality of Waldeck-Pyrmont, which gave up its independence in stages to Prussia.
free-state-of-waldeck.o: Prince Friedrich of [[s:principality-of-waldeck|Waldeck-Pyrmont]] was deposed in November 1918, and the principality became a free state with [[e:bad-arolsen|Arolsen]] as capital. Waldeck had been administered by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] under an accession treaty since 1868, so its independence was already limited.
free-state-of-waldeck.r: The free state was rural and poor, with farming and forestry in the hills around the [[e:eder-river|Eder]]. Its finances depended on Prussian support. In 1921 the inhabitants of the detached district of [[s:county-of-pyrmont|Pyrmont]] voted to join [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and Pyrmont passed to the [[e:province-of-hanover|Province of Hanover]] in 1922. The remaining state struggled to sustain its own government.
free-state-of-waldeck.e: After a treaty with [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], the Free State of Waldeck was absorbed into Prussia on 1 April 1929 and became part of the [[e:province-of-hesse-nassau|Province of Hesse-Nassau]]. It is now in the state of [[e:hesse|Hesse]].

free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.t: One of the smallest Alsatian Decapolis cities, a wine town known for its Romanesque church of Saints Peter and Paul.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.o: Rosheim, at the foot of the [[e:vosges|Vosges]] west of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], was an imperial possession under the [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]]. The town was walled in the 13th century and its rights as a free imperial city were confirmed around 1303. In 1354 it joined the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]], the alliance of ten Alsatian imperial cities under the imperial bailiff at [[s:free-imperial-city-of-haguenau|Haguenau]].
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] governed this small community of vintners, farmers and craftsmen. Its church of [[e:church-of-saints-peter-and-paul-rosheim|Saints Peter and Paul]], built in the 12th century of yellow sandstone, is one of the finest [[e:romanesque-architecture|Romanesque]] buildings in [[e:alsace|Alsace]], and the town also preserves a stone house of the same age. Rosheim remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rosheim.e: The town suffered heavily in [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years' War. After 1648 the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] came under French protection, and the [[e:treaties-of-nijmegen|Treaty of Nijmegen]] of 1679 confirmed its incorporation into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]]. It is now a small town in the [[e:bas-rhin|Bas-Rhin]] [[e:departement|department]].

french-madagascar.t: Madagascar as a French colony, from the overthrow of the Merina monarchy to the autonomous Malagasy Republic of 1958.
french-madagascar.o: After the conquest of 1895 and the end of the [[s:french-protectorate-of-madagascar|French Protectorate of Madagascar]], [[e:france|France]] annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 the governor-general [[e:joseph-gallieni|Joseph Gallieni]] abolished the Merina monarchy and exiled [[e:ranavalona-iii|Queen Ranavalona III]] to Réunion and later [[e:algeria|Algeria]], then put down the [[e:menalamba-rebellion|Menalamba rising]] and subdued the coastal peoples.
french-madagascar.r: Gallieni and his successors imposed a head tax and forced labour, promoted French over English schooling and broke the power of the Merina elite. [[e:coffee-economy|Coffee]], vanilla, [[e:cloves|cloves]] and [[e:rice|rice]] were exported, and [[s:nosy-be|Nosy Be]], [[s:diego-suarez-colony|Diego-Suarez]] and the [[e:comoro-islands|Comoros]] were attached. In 1942 British forces took the island from [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]], and it passed to the [[s:free-france|Free French]].
french-madagascar.e: The nationalist uprising of 1947 was crushed with tens of thousands of deaths. [[e:madagascar|Madagascar]] became the autonomous Malagasy Republic in October 1958 and fully independent on 26 June 1960 under President [[e:philibert-tsiranana|Philibert Tsiranana]].

former-shu.t: The kingdom founded in Sichuan by the soldier Wang Jian, a wealthy refuge for Tang scholars and poets in the turmoil after the Tang collapse.
former-shu.o: [[e:wang-jian-former-shu|Wang Jian]], a soldier from [[e:henan|Henan]] who had served in the palace army, seized [[e:chengdu|Chengdu]] in 891 and became military governor of the region. The [[s:later-tang|Tang]] made him Prince of Shu in 903. When [[e:zhu-wen|Zhu Wen]] deposed the Tang in 907, Wang Jian refused to recognise the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]] and proclaimed himself emperor.
former-shu.r: Protected by mountains, the fertile [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] basin escaped the wars of the north and prospered from [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]], salt and [[e:tea|tea]]. Many [[s:later-tang|Tang]] officials and literati took refuge at [[e:chengdu|Chengdu]], among them the poet [[e:wei-zhuang|Wei Zhuang]], who served as chief minister. The Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, after the dynasty, but reflects the court culture it fostered.
former-shu.e: [[e:wang-jian-former-shu|Wang Jian's]] son [[e:wang-yan-former-shu|Wang Yan]], who succeeded in 918, was extravagant and neglected government. In 925 a [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]] army marched in and met little resistance; Wang Yan surrendered and was killed with his family in 926 on the way to [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]]. [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] soon became independent again as [[s:later-shu|Later Shu]].

frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.t: Merovingian kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, built on the old Kingdom of the Burgundians and ruled from Chalon-sur-Saône.
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.o: The [[s:franks|Franks]] conquered the [[s:kingdom-of-the-burgundians|Kingdom of the Burgundians]] in 534. At the division of 561 [[e:chlothar-i|Chlothar I's]] son [[e:guntram|Guntram]] received [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] with [[e:orleans|Orléans]], ruling from [[e:chalon-sur-saone|Chalon-sur-Saône]]. The kingdom stretched from the [[e:loire|Loire]] to the [[e:alps|Alps]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.r: [[e:guntram|Guntram]], a long-reigning king later venerated as a saint, acted as mediator between his feuding brothers' kingdoms. [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] kept its [[e:roman-law|Roman law]] and Gallo-Roman aristocracy and its own mayor of the palace. The Irish monk [[e:columbanus|Columbanus]] founded [[e:luxeuil-abbey|Luxeuil]] there, but was expelled by King [[e:theuderic-ii|Theuderic II]] and [[e:brunhilda-of-austrasia|Brunhild]].
frankish-kingdom-of-burgundy.e: After 613 [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] was ruled together with [[s:neustria|Neustria]] by [[e:chlothar-ii|Chlothar II]] and his successors, though it kept a separate identity. It passed under [[e:pippinids|Pippinid]] control, and [[e:charles-martel|Charles Martel]] subdued it in the 730s. With Pippin's accession in 751 it became a region of the Frankish realm.

free-state-bottleneck.t: Accidental mini-state in the Rhine valley, left unoccupied between French and American zones after the First World War.
free-state-bottleneck.o: The [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]] of 1918 gave the [[e:allies|Allies]] bridgeheads on the right bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], drawn as circles of 30 kilometres around [[e:koblenz|Koblenz]] and [[e:mainz|Mainz]]. The two circles left a narrow gap near [[e:lorch-am-rhein|Lorch]] and [[e:kaub|Kaub]], cut off from unoccupied [[e:germany|Germany]] by hills, which became known from January 1919 as the Free State Bottleneck.
free-state-bottleneck.r: The area of some 17,000 people had no direct road or rail link with [[e:germany|Germany]]. [[e:lorch-am-rhein|Lorch]]'s mayor, [[e:edmund-pnischeck|Edmund Pnischeck]], headed an improvised administration. Locals smuggled goods across the hills, printed their own emergency money and, in a famous episode, hijacked a French [[e:coal|coal]] train to keep warm.
free-state-bottleneck.e: During the occupation of the [[e:ruhr|Ruhr]], French troops occupied the territory in February 1923, ending its separate existence. The area returned to German administration when the French occupation was later lifted.

frisian-freedom.t: A medieval coastal society without lords, in which Frisian farmers governed themselves through elected judges and assemblies for nearly four centuries.
frisian-freedom.o: After the Carolingian counts lost effective control of the [[e:north-sea|North Sea]] coast in the 11th and 12th centuries, the Frisian lands between the [[e:vlie|Vlie]] and the [[e:weser|Weser]] governed themselves. [[s:frisii|Frisians]] claimed their liberty came from a privilege granted by [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]], a legend that justified their refusal to accept feudal lords.
frisian-freedom.r: Each land or community chose its own judges, called redjeven or consuls, and delegates of the [[e:seven-sealands|Seven Sealands]] met at the [[e:upstalsboom|Upstalsboom]] near [[e:aurich|Aurich]]. [[s:frisii|Frisians]] built dykes and terps, raised [[e:cattle|cattle]] and traded by sea, and wrote down their own laws in Old Frisian. There were no knights or castles in the usual sense, but powerful chieftains, the hoofdelingen, rose in the 14th century.
frisian-freedom.e: Feuds between the [[e:schieringers|Schieringers]] and [[e:vetkopers|Vetkopers]] weakened the [[s:frisii|Frisians]] in the 15th century. [[e:east-frisia|East Frisia]] came under the [[e:house-of-cirksena|Cirksena]] counts in 1464, and in 1498 [[e:maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Maximilian]] made [[e:albert-iii-duke-of-saxony|Albert of Saxony]] governor of [[s:lordship-of-frisia|Friesland]], ending the freedom west of the Ems and creating the Lordship of [[e:frisia|Frisia]].

free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.t: Swabian imperial city, perhaps the oldest Hohenstaufen town, home of the Parler family of master builders and long famous for gold and silver work.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.o: Gmünd is often called the oldest [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] town, founded around 1162 near the family's ancestral castle on the Hohenstaufen hill. After the execution of [[e:conradin|Conradin]], the last Hohenstaufen, in 1268, the town was not claimed by any prince and became an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.r: A council of patricians and later [[e:guild|guilds]] governed the city. [[e:heinrich-parler|Heinrich Parler]] began the [[e:holy-cross-minster|Holy Cross Minster]] there in the 14th century, one of the first German hall churches in the late Gothic style, and his son [[e:peter-parler|Peter Parler]] went on to build [[e:prague|Prague]] Cathedral. Gold and [[e:silver|silver]] smithing and the making of rosaries were its main trades. Gmünd remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-gmund.e: The city lost its freedom in 1802, when Württemberg annexed it. It remains a centre of the goldsmith's and silversmith's trade and is now a town in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]], with the [[e:holy-cross-minster|Holy Cross Minster]] at its heart.

free-imperial-city-of-lindau.t: Island city in Lake Constance, a trading gateway to Italy and Switzerland and one of four cities that signed the Tetrapolitan Confession in 1530.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.o: Lindau grew around a convent of noble canonesses founded on an island in [[e:lake-constance|Lake Constance]]. The town became an important market and port, and after the [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] era it gained recognition as an imperial city, around 1275, gradually limiting the convent's rights.
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed. Lindau thrived on trade over the lake and through the Alpine passes to [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]], served by the Lindau messenger service. The city hosted an [[e:imperial-diet|imperial diet]] in 1496. It accepted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and in 1530 joined [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]], [[e:konstanz|Constance]] and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-memmingen|Memmingen]] in presenting the [[e:tetrapolitan-confession|Tetrapolitan Confession]], later adopting [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]].
free-imperial-city-of-lindau.e: In 1802 Lindau went to Prince Bretzenheim, then to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1804 and to [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] in 1805. It remains Bavarian, Bavaria's only town on [[e:lake-constance|Lake Constance]], linked to the mainland by bridge and railway causeway.

free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.t: Swabian imperial city of the Fugger and Welser bankers, where the Augsburg Confession was read in 1530 and the Peace of Augsburg made in 1555.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.o: [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] grew from the Roman provincial capital of [[e:augusta-vindelicorum|Augusta Vindelicorum]] and was ruled for centuries by its [[e:bishop|bishops]]. Its citizens won increasing self-government, and in 1276 [[e:rudolf-i-of-germany|King Rudolf I]] confirmed their town law, making Augsburg an imperial city independent of the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-augsburg|Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg]].
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed after the guild revolution of 1368. Textile production and banking made [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] one of [[e:europe|Europe's]] richest cities; the [[e:fugger-family|Fuggers]] financed emperors and founded the Fuggerei social housing in 1516. The [[e:augsburg-confession|Augsburg Confession]] was presented at the diet of 1530, and the [[e:peace-of-augsburg|Peace of Augsburg]] of 1555 recognised [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]. After 1648 Catholics and Protestants shared offices equally.
free-imperial-city-of-augsburg.e: [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]] lost its freedom in 1806 when it was annexed by the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. It remains a major Bavarian city, and the Peace Festival of 8 August, held since 1650, is still a local holiday.

free-state-of-saxony.t: Republican Saxony between the monarchy and East German centralisation, an industrial state of left-wing politics and later Soviet rule.
free-state-of-saxony.o: [[e:frederick-augustus-iii-of-saxony|King Frederick Augustus III]] abdicated in November 1918, and workers' and soldiers' councils briefly took power. A Landtag was elected in 1919, and in 1920 a constitution established [[e:saxony|Saxony]] as a free state within the [[s:weimar-republic|Weimar Republic]], with [[e:dresden|Dresden]] as capital.
free-state-of-saxony.r: [[e:saxony|Saxony's]] industry made it a stronghold of the Social Democrats and Communists. In 1923 the government of [[e:erich-zeigner|Erich Zeigner]], including Communists, was deposed by the federal government with troops. The [[e:nazism|Nazis]] took control in 1933, with [[e:martin-mutschmann|Martin Mutschmann]] as Reich governor. [[e:dresden|Dresden]] was devastated by Allied bombing in February 1945, and Saxony fell in the Soviet occupation zone.
free-state-of-saxony.e: After 1945 [[e:saxony|Saxony]] was restored as a Land in the Soviet zone and in 1949 in the [[e:east-germany|German Democratic Republic]]. In 1952 the GDR abolished the [[e:states-of-germany|Länder]], dividing Saxony into the districts of [[e:dresden|Dresden]], [[e:leipzig|Leipzig]] and [[e:chemnitz|Chemnitz]] (renamed Karl-Marx-Stadt in 1953); it was re-established in 1990.

free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.t: Lake Constance imperial city whose grain market fed the region and whose walls held off Swedish sieges in the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.o: Überlingen was a royal estate and [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] town on the north shore of [[e:lake-constance|Lake Constance]], with a harbour serving the grain trade across the lake. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen around 1268, it became an imperial city, confirmed by later kings, with a small territory of nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.r: A council dominated by [[e:guild|guilds]] ruled. Its grain market supplied [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] and the lake region, and wine was another source of wealth. The town remained Catholic and loyal to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]], and in 1632 and 1634 it withstood Swedish sieges. Its large Gothic minster of St. Nicholas holds a famous carved high altar by [[e:jorg-zurn|Jörg Zürn]].
free-imperial-city-of-uberlingen.e: Überlingen lost its freedom in 1803 when it was annexed by [[e:baden|Baden]]. In the 19th century its mineral spring made it a spa and resort town, and it is now in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]], its minster and walls well preserved.

four-macedonian-republics.t: The four self-governing districts into which Rome split the old kingdom of Macedon after Pydna, a short-lived experiment that ended in revolt and annexation.
four-macedonian-republics.o: After defeating [[e:perseus-of-macedon|Perseus]] at [[e:battle-of-pydna|Pydna]] in 168 BCE, [[e:rome|Rome]] abolished the [[s:antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia|Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia]]. In 167 BCE [[e:lucius-aemilius-paullus-macedonicus|Lucius Aemilius Paullus]] announced the settlement at [[s:amphipolis|Amphipolis]]: [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] was to be 'free' but divided into four republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, [[e:thessaloniki|Thessalonica]], [[s:pella|Pella]] and [[e:pelagonia|Pelagonia]].
four-macedonian-republics.r: Each republic had elected magistrates and a council, but contact between them was restricted: citizens could not marry or own land across the borders. The Macedonians paid [[e:rome|Rome]] half the taxes they had paid their kings, the royal gold and [[e:silver|silver]] mines were closed until 158 BCE and [[e:timber|timber]] from the royal forests was banned. The first meris struck silver coins showing [[e:artemis|Artemis]].
four-macedonian-republics.e: Resentment and disorder grew. In 149 BCE [[e:andriscus|Andriscus]], claiming to be a son of [[e:perseus-of-macedon|Perseus]], reunited [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] briefly as king. [[e:quintus-caecilius-metellus-macedonicus|Quintus Caecilius Metellus]] defeated him in 148 BCE, and [[e:macedonia-roman-province|Macedonia]] became a Roman province in 146 BCE, with the [[e:via-egnatia|Via Egnatia]] later binding it together.

falerii.t: Chief city of the Faliscans, a people who spoke a language close to Latin but lived within Etruscan culture, destroyed by Rome in 241 BCE.
falerii.o: Falerii, later called Falerii Veteres, stood on a steep tufa plateau at modern [[e:civita-castellana|Civita Castellana]] in the [[e:ager-faliscus|Ager Faliscus]], between the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] and [[e:monte-cimino|Monte Cimino]]. It developed from [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]] settlements of the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. The Faliscans spoke Faliscan, an Italic language closely related to [[e:latin|Latin]], though their art, cults and politics were tied to [[e:etruria|Etruria]].
falerii.r: Falerii was famous for the cult of [[e:juno-curitis|Juno Curitis]], whose festival [[e:ovid|Ovid]] described, and for its temples decorated with fine terracottas. Its workshops produced Faliscan red-figure vases in the 4th century BCE. The city usually allied with [[s:veii|Veii]] against [[e:rome|Rome]]; Roman legend tells how [[e:marcus-furius-camillus|Camillus]], besieging it in 394 BCE, sent back a schoolmaster who tried to hand over his pupils, and the Faliscans surrendered in admiration.
falerii.e: After further wars Falerii revolted in 241 BCE, just after the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]], and was crushed within days. [[e:rome|Rome]] destroyed the hilltop city and moved its people to [[e:falerii-novi|Falerii Novi]] on open ground about 6 km away, whose walls still stand. The old site was resettled in the [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]] as [[e:civita-castellana|Civita Castellana]].

free-state-of-icaria.t: Tiny independent republic declared on the Aegean island of Icaria in 1912 after islanders expelled the Ottoman garrison, lasting months until union with Greece.
free-state-of-icaria.o: [[e:ikaria|Icaria]], a mountainous island west of [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]], was under Ottoman rule when [[e:italy|Italy's]] war with the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] weakened Turkish control in the [[e:aegean|Aegean]]. On 17 July 1912 the islanders, led by the doctor [[e:ioannis-malachias|Ioannis Malachias]], rose against the small Ottoman garrison, forced its surrender and proclaimed the Free State of Icaria.
free-state-of-icaria.r: The new state set up a provisional government at [[e:agios-kirykos|Agios Kirykos]], adopted its own flag and issued postage stamps. It lacked money, an army and any outside recognition, and the islanders, who lived by farming, herding and emigration, hoped for annexation by [[e:greece|Greece]] rather than lasting independence.
free-state-of-icaria.e: When the [[e:first-balkan-war|First Balkan War]] began, the Greek navy arrived in November 1912 and the island joined the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]]. The episode lasted about five months and is still commemorated on [[e:ikaria|Icaria]] every July.

free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.t: Democratic successor of the Kingdom of Württemberg, a well-governed Weimar state that was split by the occupying powers in 1945.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.o: In November 1918 [[e:william-ii-of-wurttemberg|King William II]] abdicated, and a provisional government of Social Democrats and [[e:independent-social-democratic-party-of-germany|Independents]] declared a republic in [[e:stuttgart|Stuttgart]]. A constitution adopted in 1919 created the Free People's State of Württemberg.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.r: Württemberg had a balanced economy of small farms and skilled industry, with companies such as [[e:robert-bosch-gmbh|Bosch]] and [[e:daimler-motoren-gesellschaft|Daimler]]. After governments led by Social Democrats and liberals, the state was led by conservatives and from 1928 by the Centre's [[e:eugen-bolz|Eugen Bolz]], who was later executed for his part in the resistance to [[e:adolf-hitler|Hitler]]. After 1933 the Nazi Reich governor [[e:wilhelm-murr|Wilhelm Murr]] ruled the state.
free-peoples-state-of-wurttemberg.e: After 1945 the state was divided by the occupying powers: the northern part, in the American zone, joined northern [[e:baden|Baden]] as Württemberg-Baden, and the southern part, under the French, became Württemberg-Hohenzollern. They merged into [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]] in 1952.

funj-sultanate.t: The Sultanate of Sennar, which replaced Christian Alodia and ruled the middle Nile for three centuries, spreading Islam across Sudan.
funj-sultanate.o: In 1504 the [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Funj]] leader [[e:amara-dunqas|Amara Dunqas]] founded Sennar on the [[e:blue-nile|Blue Nile]]. Allied with the Arab chief [[e:abdallah-jamma|Abdallah Jamma]] of the [[s:abdallab-sheikhdom|Abdallab Sheikhdom]], the Funj destroyed [[s:alodia|Alodia]] and its capital [[e:soba|Soba]], establishing a sultanate that dominated the [[e:gezira|Gezira]] and the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley north to the third cataract.
funj-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled through [[e:vassal|vassal]] lords, among them the [[s:abdallab-sheikhdom|Abdallab]], who held the north. [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Sennar]] grew rich on gold, slaves and caravan trade with [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]]. [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teachers and Islamic schools spread [[e:islam|Islam]] and Arabic among the population. Badi II created a slave army, and later sultans were dominated by the [[e:hamaj|Hamaj]] regents from 1761.
funj-sultanate.e: Weakened by civil wars, [[e:funj-sultanate-of-sennar|Sennar]] fell to Ismail Pasha's army in 1821 as [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]] conquered [[e:sudan|Sudan]], creating the [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]]. The last sultan, Badi VII, submitted without a fight.

free-state-of-anhalt.t: Small central German republic that hosted the Bauhaus at Dessau and in 1932 became the first state with a Nazi head of government.
free-state-of-anhalt.o: Duke [[e:joachim-ernst-duke-of-anhalt|Joachim Ernst]]'s regent abdicated in November 1918, and the [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] became a free state, with a democratic constitution adopted in 1919 and [[e:dessau|Dessau]] as capital.
free-state-of-anhalt.r: [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] was governed by Social Democratic coalitions for most of the 1920s. Its industries included the [[e:junkers|Junkers]] aircraft works and chemical plants at [[e:bitterfeld|Bitterfeld]] nearby. In 1925 the [[e:bauhaus|Bauhaus]] moved from [[e:weimar|Weimar]] to [[e:dessau|Dessau]], where [[e:walter-gropius|Walter Gropius]] designed its new building. After the [[e:nazi-party|Nazis]] won the 1932 state election, [[e:alfred-freyberg|Alfred Freyberg]] became the first Nazi minister-president of a German state, and the Bauhaus was forced out that year.
free-state-of-anhalt.e: The [[e:nazi-party|Nazis]] subordinated [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] to a Reich governor. In 1945 it was occupied and placed in the Soviet zone, where it was merged with the Prussian [[e:province-of-saxony|Province of Saxony]] to form the province, later Land, of [[e:saxony-anhalt|Saxony-Anhalt]].

free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.t: Tiny imperial city on the north shore of Lake Constance that was merged with a neighbouring priory to form the town of Friedrichshafen in 1811.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.o: Buchhorn grew on the north shore of [[e:lake-constance|Lake Constance]] as a fishing and market settlement under the counts of Buchhorn and later the [[e:house-of-welf|Guelphs]] and [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]]. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I around 1275.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.r: Buchhorn was one of the smallest imperial cities, with a council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and a tiny territory. It lived from fishing, lake shipping and trade across the lake to [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]], and its market served the surrounding countryside. It remained Catholic and depended on alliances with other Swabian cities and on Austrian goodwill.
free-imperial-city-of-buchhorn.e: [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] annexed Buchhorn in 1802 and passed it to Württemberg in 1810. In 1811 [[e:frederick-i-of-wurttemberg|King Frederick I of Württemberg]] merged it with the neighbouring Hofen priory to create Friedrichshafen, later the home of the [[e:ferdinand-von-zeppelin|Zeppelin]] airships.

french-protectorate-of-tunisia.t: Tunisia under French rule from 1881, where the bey reigned but a French resident-general governed, until independence in 1956.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.o: Using border raids as a pretext, [[e:france|France]] invaded the [[s:beylik-of-tunis|Beylik of Tunis]] in 1881 and forced [[e:muhammad-iii-as-sadiq|Muhammad as-Sadiq Bey]] to sign the [[e:treaty-of-bardo|Treaty of Bardo]]. The [[e:la-marsa-convention|La Marsa Convention]] of 1883 placed internal administration under French control, with the bey retained as nominal sovereign.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.r: A French resident-general held real power, with French officials running finance, public works and justice for Europeans. French and Italian settlers acquired farmland for olives, vines and grain, and phosphate mining expanded. Tunisian nationalism grew through the [[e:destour|Destour]] party, founded in 1920, and [[e:habib-bourguiba|Habib Bourguiba's]] [[e:neo-destour|Neo-Destour]] from 1934. [[e:moncef-bey|Moncef Bey]] was deposed by the French in 1943.
french-protectorate-of-tunisia.e: After armed resistance and negotiations, [[e:france|France]] granted internal autonomy in 1955 and full independence in March 1956. [[e:muhammad-al-amin-bey|Lamine Bey]] became king of the [[s:kingdom-of-tunisia|Kingdom of Tunisia]], with [[e:habib-bourguiba|Bourguiba]] as prime minister.

fib.t: A Pictish province between the Tay and the Forth, the ancestor of the Kingdom of Fife, named in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
fib.o: Fib appears among the seven Pictish provinces named after the legendary sons of [[e:cruithne-legendary-king|Cruithne]]. Its territory corresponded broadly to modern [[e:fife|Fife]] and [[e:kinross-shire|Kinross]], between the [[e:firth-of-tay|Firth of Tay]] and the [[e:firth-of-forth|Firth of Forth]].
fib.r: Nothing is known of its rulers in the Pictish period. The peninsula was fertile, and [[e:st-andrews|St Andrews]], known earlier as Cennrigmonaid, became one of the leading Pictish churches, receiving relics of [[e:andrew-the-apostle|Saint Andrew]] by tradition in the 8th century.
fib.e: Fib became the earldom of [[e:fife|Fife]] within the [[s:kingdom-of-scotland|Kingdom of Scotland]], whose earls held the right to enthrone the king at [[e:scone-scotland|Scone]]. Fife still calls itself 'the Kingdom'.

free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.t: Swabian imperial city on Roman foundations, seat of an imperial court and for over a century an ally of the Swiss Confederacy.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.o: Rottweil grew on the site of the Roman town of [[e:arae-flaviae|Arae Flaviae]] on the upper [[e:neckar|Neckar]]. A royal estate in the Carolingian period, it was refounded by the [[e:house-of-zahringen|Zähringen]] and [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] and became an imperial city after their fall, by around 1268.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.r: The city was home to the [[e:imperial-court-of-rottweil|Imperial Court of Rottweil]], which heard cases from across south-western [[e:germany|Germany]]. A council with strong [[e:guild|guild]] participation governed it, and it acquired one of the largest territories of any Swabian imperial city. In 1519 it concluded a perpetual alliance with the [[s:old-swiss-confederacy|Old Swiss Confederacy]], as an associate member. It remained Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-rottweil.e: Rottweil lost its freedom in 1802 when Württemberg annexed it, and the imperial court was abolished. Its Swabian-Alemannic carnival, the [[e:swabian-alemannic-fastnacht|Fasnet]], remains famous, and it is now a town in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]].

faroese-commonwealth.t: Self-governing Norse community of the Faroe Islands, ruled by its assembly at Tinganes until it came under the Norwegian crown.
faroese-commonwealth.o: Norse settlers reached the [[e:faroe-islands|Faroe Islands]] in the early 9th century; the Irish monk [[e:dicuil|Dicuil]] wrote around 825 that Irish hermits there had been driven out by Northmen raiders. The settlers were farmers and herders, many from western [[e:norway|Norway]], and some with Gaelic links from the [[e:british-isles|British Isles]].
faroese-commonwealth.r: The islanders governed themselves through the [[e:logting|Alting]] at [[e:tinganes|Tinganes]], in what is now [[e:torshavn|Tórshavn]], one of the oldest parliamentary sites in the world. Sheep farming, fowling and fishing supported the population. The [[e:faereyinga-saga|Færeyinga saga]] tells how [[e:sigmundur-brestisson|Sigmundur Brestisson]] brought [[e:christianity|Christianity]] around 999 for King [[e:olaf-tryggvason|Olaf Tryggvason]], opposed by the chieftain [[e:trondur-i-gotu|Tróndur í Gøtu]].
faroese-commonwealth.e: By about 1035 the islands paid tax to the Norwegian king and became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]]. They later passed to [[s:denmark-norway|Denmark-Norway]] and remained with [[e:denmark|Denmark]] after 1814. The [[e:logting|Løgting]] still meets in [[e:torshavn|Tórshavn]], and the [[e:faroe-islands|Faroe Islands]] are a self-governing part of the Danish realm.

first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.t: The first Ibadi state in Oman, an elected imamate centred on Nizwa that set the pattern for Omani religious government for a thousand years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.o: In 751 the Omani [[e:ibadism|Ibadis]] elected al-[[e:al-julanda-ibn-masud|Julanda ibn Mas'ud]] as their first [[e:imam|imam]], but he was killed the next year by an army of the new [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]]. After decades under local chiefs, the [[e:imamate|imamate]] was restored in 793 with the election of Muhammad ibn Affan, followed by Warith ibn Ka'b, and lasted a century.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.r: [[e:imam|Imams]] were chosen by the learned and leading men and could be deposed if they broke the law, an ideal of accountable leadership central to [[e:ibadism|Ibadism]]. [[e:nizwa|Nizwa]] became the capital and a centre of scholarship. [[e:oman|Oman]] controlled the sea trade of the [[e:persian-gulf|Gulf]] through [[e:sohar|Sohar]], while the falaj irrigation channels supported date farming in the interior. [[e:al-salt-ibn-malik|al-Salt ibn Malik]] ruled for over thirty years.
first-ibadi-imamate-of-oman.e: The deposition of [[e:al-salt-ibn-malik|al-Salt ibn Malik]] in 886 split Omani scholars into rival schools and led to civil war. In 893 the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid]] governor of [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], Muhammad ibn Nur, invaded, sacked [[e:nizwa|Nizwa]] and ended the [[e:imamate|imamate]], though Ibadi [[e:imam|imams]] reappeared repeatedly later.

finnish-socialist-workers-republic.t: Red Finland, the revolutionary government that held southern Finland during the civil war of 1918 before its defeat by the Whites and Germany.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.o: Tensions after independence erupted into civil war in January 1918. On 28 January the [[e:red-guards-finland|Red Guards]] seized Helsinki, and the [[e:finnish-peoples-delegation|Finnish People's Delegation]], chaired by [[e:kullervo-manner|Kullervo Manner]], took power in the industrial south. In late February it was proclaimed the Finnish Socialist Workers' Republic.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.r: The Reds controlled the cities and industrial centres of southern [[s:republic-of-finland|Finland]], including Helsinki, [[e:tampere|Tampere]], [[e:turku|Turku]] and [[e:vyborg|Viipuri]]. Their draft constitution mixed socialist ideas with parliamentary democracy, and they received arms from [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]]. Both sides committed terror, and the Red administration struggled with food shortages and military weakness.
finnish-socialist-workers-republic.e: The White army under [[e:carl-gustaf-emil-mannerheim|Mannerheim]] won the decisive [[e:battle-of-tampere|Battle of Tampere]] in April 1918, while German troops took Helsinki. Red [[s:republic-of-finland|Finland]] collapsed in May, and about 80,000 Reds were held in prison camps, where some 12,000 died. Its leaders fled to [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]] and founded the Communist Party of [[e:finland|Finland]].

free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.t: A northern Alsatian imperial city that grew around a powerful Benedictine abbey and joined the Decapolis before passing to France.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.o: Wissembourg grew around the Benedictine abbey of [[e:wissembourg-abbey|Saints Peter and Paul]], founded in the 7th century on the [[e:lauter-rhine|Lauter]], where the monk [[e:otfrid-of-weissenburg|Otfrid]] wrote his [[e:old-high-german|Old High German]] Gospel Harmony in the 9th century. The townspeople slowly freed themselves from the abbot's lordship, and by the early 14th century the town ranked as a free imperial city. In 1354 it was a founding member of the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]].
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed the town, which lived from wine, crafts and the road between [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]] and the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]]. The abbey remained a rival authority; it became a provostry in 1524 and was united with the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-speyer|Prince-Bishopric of Speyer]] in 1546. The [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] won a following among the townspeople, while the abbey stayed Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg.e: Repeatedly fought over in the 17th century, Wissembourg came under French protection after 1648, and annexation by the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]] was confirmed by the [[e:treaties-of-nijmegen|Treaty of Nijmegen]] in 1679. The exiled Polish king [[e:stanislaw-leszczynski|Stanisław Leszczyński]] later lived there. It is now a town in the [[e:bas-rhin|Bas-Rhin]] [[e:departement|department]].

free-state-of-prussia.t: Republican Prussia, Germany's largest state and a democratic bulwark under Social Democrats until a coup in 1932.
free-state-of-prussia.o: With William II's abdication in November 1918 the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]] became a republic. A constitution of 1920 created the Free State of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], covering about three-fifths of [[e:germany|Germany's]] territory and population, from [[e:east-prussia|East Prussia]] to the [[e:rhineland|Rhineland]], though it lost territory to [[e:poland|Poland]], [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]] and [[e:denmark|Denmark]] under the [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]].
free-state-of-prussia.r: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] was governed for most of the 1920s by a coalition of Social Democrats, the Catholic Centre and liberals under Minister-President [[e:otto-braun|Otto Braun]], with a police force loyal to the republic. In July 1932 Chancellor [[e:franz-von-papen|Franz von Papen]] removed the Prussian government by decree, the [[e:prussian-coup-of-1932|Preußenschlag]]. Under the [[e:nazi-party|Nazis]], [[e:hermann-goring|Hermann Göring]] became minister-president and Prussia lost its separate statehood in practice.
free-state-of-prussia.e: After 1945 [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia's]] eastern territories passed to [[e:poland|Poland]] and the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], and its Germans were expelled. The [[s:allied-occupied-germany|Allied Control Council]] formally abolished Prussia by Law No. 46 on 25 February 1947.

four-oirat.t: The confederation of western Mongol peoples that rivalled the Chinggisid khans for two centuries and captured a Ming emperor at Tumu in 1449.
four-oirat.o: The [[e:oirats|Oirats]] were forest and steppe peoples of north-western [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]] who had joined the [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] early. After the fall of the [[s:yuan-dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] in 1368 they formed a union of four main groups, usually listed as the [[e:choros-oirats|Choros]], [[e:torghut|Torghut]], [[e:dorbet|Dörbet]] and [[s:khoshut-khanate|Khoshut]], and challenged the [[s:northern-yuan|Northern Yuan]] khans for leadership of the steppe.
four-oirat.r: The confederation was governed by an assembly of chiefs, and its leaders, not being descendants of [[e:genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]], usually ruled through puppet khans. [[e:toghon-taishi|Toghon]] and his son [[e:esen-taishi|Esen]] built [[e:oirats|Oirat]] power in the 15th century; Esen defeated and captured the [[e:ming-empire|Ming]] emperor [[e:zhengtong-emperor|Zhengtong]] at [[e:tumu-crisis|Tumu]] in 1449 and briefly took the title of khan himself before being killed in 1455.
four-oirat.e: Pushed west by [[e:dayan-khan|Dayan Khan]] and [[e:altan-khan|Altan Khan]], the [[e:oirats|Oirats]] moved towards [[s:dzungar-khanate|Dzungaria]] in the 16th century and adopted [[e:gelug|Gelug Buddhism]]. In the 1630s the confederation divided into the Dzungar Khanate, the [[s:kalmyk-khanate|Kalmyk Khanate]] on the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the [[s:khoshut-khanate|Khoshut Khanate]] in [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]].

fatagar-sultanate.t: A small medieval Muslim state in central Ethiopia, caught between the Christian emperors and the sultanates of Ifat and Adal.
fatagar-sultanate.o: Fatagar is known from Arabic and Ethiopian sources as a Muslim region lying between [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]] and the [[e:awash-river|Awash]] river, east of modern [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]]. It appears in the 13th century and became a tributary of the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] under [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] in the 14th century.
fatagar-sultanate.r: Little is recorded about its rulers or institutions. It was a farming and trading area on the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] to [[e:zeila|Zeila]], and its population was partly Muslim and partly Christian, with both mosques and churches. It served at times as a royal camping ground of the emperors.
fatagar-sultanate.e: Fatagar was overrun during the [[e:jihad|jihad]] of [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] in the 1530s, and Oromo migrations in the mid-16th century then swept away the old political order. The name fell out of use as the area became part of [[e:oromo|Oromo]] [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]].

fidenae.t: Small town on the Tiber just north of Rome, allied with Veii, which Rome fought for repeatedly and finally destroyed in 426 BCE.
fidenae.o: Fidenae stood on a hill above the left bank of the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]], about 8 km north of [[e:rome|Rome]], opposite the Etruscan city of [[s:veii|Veii]]. It was a [[e:latin|Latin]] town, though [[e:livy|Livy]] says it had Etruscan connections, and settlement there goes back to the early [[e:iron-age|Iron Age]]. Its position on the river and the [[e:via-salaria|Via Salaria]] made it strategically vital.
fidenae.r: Little is known of its government. Roman tradition tells of repeated wars from the time of [[e:romulus|Romulus]], as Fidenae shifted between [[e:rome|Rome]] and [[s:veii|Veii]]. In 438 BCE it went over to [[e:lars-tolumnius|Lars Tolumnius]] of Veii and killed Roman envoys; the Roman officer [[e:aulus-cornelius-cossus|Aulus Cornelius Cossus]] killed Tolumnius in single combat and dedicated his armour as the spolia opima.
fidenae.e: In 426 BCE the dictator [[e:mamercus-aemilius-mamercinus|Mamercus Aemilius]] captured and destroyed Fidenae, and its land became Roman. It survived only as a village; under [[e:tiberius|Tiberius]], in 27 CE, the collapse of a wooden amphitheatre there reportedly killed thousands, as [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] records.

free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.t: Danube city of Roman origin, a great medieval trading hub and from 1663 the permanent seat of the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.o: Regensburg grew from the Roman [[e:legion|legionary]] fortress of [[e:castra-regina|Castra Regina]] and became the seat of the Bavarian dukes and a [[e:bishop|bishop]]. Its merchants traded from [[e:venice|Venice]] to [[e:kyiv|Kiev]], and the Stone Bridge over the [[e:danube|Danube]] was built in the 1130s and 1140s. In 1245 Frederick II granted the city self-government, making it an imperial city.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.r: Patrician merchant families, whose tower houses still stand, ruled through the council. The [[e:bishop|bishop]], several imperial abbeys and the city shared the town. Trade declined in the 15th century, and Regensburg briefly submitted to [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]] from 1486 to 1492. It adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1542. From 1663 to 1806 it hosted the [[e:imperial-diet|Perpetual Imperial Diet]], the Empire's standing assembly.
free-imperial-city-of-regensburg.e: In 1803 the city became part of the [[e:principality-of-regensburg|Principality of Regensburg]] under [[e:karl-theodor-von-dalberg|Karl Theodor von Dalberg]], and in 1810 it passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. Its medieval old town is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

free-imperial-city-of-speyer.t: A Rhineland cathedral city that hosted imperial diets and the Imperial Chamber Court and gave Protestantism its name in 1529.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.o: Speyer, the Roman Noviomagus, was the burial place of the Salian emperors, whose cathedral rose there from 1030. The [[e:burghers|burghers]] gradually wrested power from the [[e:bishop|bishop]], helped by [[e:henry-v-holy-roman-emperor|Henry V]]'s charter of 1111, and in 1294 the bishop gave up most of his remaining rights, leaving the city self-governing under the emperor alone.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.r: Patricians and later the [[e:guild|guilds]] shared power in the council. The city hosted some fifty [[e:imperial-diet|imperial diets]]; at the 1529 diet the Lutheran estates issued the 'protestation' that gave Protestants their name. From 1527 to 1689 the [[e:imperial-chamber-court|Imperial Chamber Court]], the empire's highest court, sat in Speyer. The city turned Lutheran, while the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-speyer|Prince-Bishopric of Speyer]] kept the cathedral Catholic.
free-imperial-city-of-speyer.e: In 1689 French troops burned Speyer during the [[e:nine-years-war|Nine Years' War]], and the court moved to [[s:free-imperial-city-of-wetzlar|Wetzlar]]. [[e:french-first-republic|Revolutionary France]] occupied the city in 1792 and annexed it in 1797. After 1816 it was the capital of the [[e:bavarian-palatinate|Bavarian Palatinate]], and it now lies in [[e:rhineland-palatinate|Rhineland-Palatinate]].

free-state-of-mecklenburg.t: Mecklenburg reunited by the Nazis in 1934, which after 1945 became a Land of the Soviet zone and the GDR until its abolition in 1952.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.o: On 1 January 1934 a Reich law merged the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] and the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]] into a single Land of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]], with [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] as capital, ending the division that dated from 1701.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.r: Under the [[e:nazi-party|Nazis]] the state was run by Reich governor [[e:friedrich-hildebrandt|Friedrich Hildebrandt]]. Rostock's [[e:heinkel|Heinkel]] and [[e:arado-flugzeugwerke|Arado]] aircraft works made it a target of Allied bombing. In 1945 it was occupied by Soviet and British forces and placed in the Soviet zone, gaining western [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] and receiving many expellees. A land reform in 1945 broke up the large estates.
free-state-of-mecklenburg.e: Known as [[e:mecklenburg-vorpommern|Mecklenburg-Vorpommern]] until 1947, the Land became part of the [[e:east-germany|German Democratic Republic]] in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of [[s:lordship-of-rostock|Rostock]], [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] and [[e:neubrandenburg|Neubrandenburg]]; the state was re-established in 1990 as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

federal-republic-of-germany.t: Post-war German democracy, founded in the western zones in 1949 and enlarged by reunification in 1990.
federal-republic-of-germany.o: The three western occupation zones were combined, and a parliamentary council drafted the [[e:basic-law-for-the-federal-republic-of-germany|Basic Law]], which came into force on 23 May 1949. [[e:konrad-adenauer|Konrad Adenauer]] became the first chancellor, with [[e:bonn|Bonn]] as provisional capital, while the Soviet zone became the [[e:east-germany|German Democratic Republic]].
federal-republic-of-germany.r: Under the social market economy of [[e:ludwig-erhard|Ludwig Erhard]], [[e:west-germany|West Germany]] experienced the [[e:wirtschaftswunder|Wirtschaftswunder]]. It joined [[e:nato|NATO]] in 1955 and was a founding member of the [[e:european-economic-community|European Economic Community]] in 1957. Willy Brandt's [[e:ostpolitik|Ostpolitik]] eased relations with the East. The federal system gives strong powers to the [[e:states-of-germany|Länder]], and a Constitutional Court guards the [[e:basic-law-for-the-federal-republic-of-germany|Basic Law]].
federal-republic-of-germany.e: After the fall of the [[e:berlin-wall|Berlin Wall]] in 1989, the [[e:east-germany|GDR]] joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990 under [[e:helmut-kohl|Helmut Kohl]]. [[e:berlin|Berlin]] became the capital, and [[e:germany|Germany]] is today the [[e:european-union|European Union's]] most populous member and largest economy.

french-protectorate-of-madagascar.t: The French protectorate imposed on the Merina monarchy of Madagascar, a step between independence and outright colonial conquest.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.o: [[e:france|France]] fought the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]] in the [[e:franco-hova-war|Franco-Hova War]] of 1883-1885. The treaty of December 1885 gave France control over [[e:madagascar|Madagascar's]] foreign relations, the bay of [[s:diego-suarez-colony|Diego-Suarez]] and a resident-general at [[e:antananarivo|Antananarivo]], though the Merina government kept internal power.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.r: [[e:ranavalona-iii|Queen Ranavalona III]] and her prime minister and husband [[e:rainilaiarivony|Rainilaiarivony]] continued to govern through a modernised administration, a Protestant state church and an army. They disputed French claims to a full [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised French rights only in 1890. Debts from the war indemnity weakened the monarchy.
french-protectorate-of-madagascar.e: In 1895 a French expedition marched on [[e:antananarivo|Antananarivo]], which fell in September. The [[e:menalamba-rebellion|Menalamba rising]] followed, and [[e:france|France]] annexed the island in 1896. In February 1897 General Gallieni abolished the monarchy and exiled the queen, making the island the colony of [[s:french-madagascar|French Madagascar]].

french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.t: The last name of France's colony in Djibouti, adopted in 1967 to stress its Afar and Issa peoples, before independence in 1977.
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.o: After a referendum in March 1967, in which a majority voted to remain French amid protests and allegations of fraud, [[s:french-somaliland|French Somaliland]] was renamed the French Territory of the [[e:afar|Afars]] and the [[e:issa-clan|Issas]]. The name aimed to emphasise the Afar community, which [[e:france|France]] favoured over the Issa [[e:somalis|Somalis]], who were suspected of favouring union with [[s:somalia|Somalia]].
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.r: [[e:france|France]] governed through a high commissioner and a local government headed by the [[e:afar|Afar]] politician [[e:ali-aref-bourhan|Ali Aref Bourhan]]. Restrictions on residence in the capital, enforced with a barrier around [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]] city, targeted [[e:somalis|Somali]] migrants. The port and the railway to [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] remained the economic base, and the French military kept a large garrison. Nationalists such as [[e:hassan-gouled-aptidon|Hassan Gouled Aptidon]] pressed for independence, and in 1976 a hostage crisis at [[e:loyada-hostage-crisis|Loyada]] drew world attention.
french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-is.e: In May 1977 voters overwhelmingly approved independence, and on 27 June 1977 the territory became the [[s:djibouti|Republic of Djibouti]], with [[e:hassan-gouled-aptidon|Hassan Gouled Aptidon]] as president.

five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.t: Five fortified Danish towns of the east Midlands, Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham and Stamford, that formed the core of Viking rule south of the Humber.
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.o: After the [[e:great-heathen-army|Great Heathen Army]] partitioned [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] in 877, Danish warbands settled the east [[e:midlands|Midlands]] around fortified centres. Each borough was the base of a jarl and his army, controlling the surrounding district, in an area later known as part of the [[e:danelaw|Danelaw]].
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.r: The boroughs were military and trading centres that grew into towns, with Danish law, land units and many Scandinavian place-names in -by and -thorpe. They acted together at times, but there is no evidence of a single ruler. The settlers soon adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]].
five-boroughs-of-the-danelaw.e: [[e:aethelflaed|Aethelflaed]] of [[s:kingdom-of-mercia|Mercia]] and [[e:edward-the-elder|Edward the Elder]] took [[e:derby|Derby]], [[e:leicester|Leicester]], [[e:nottingham|Nottingham]] and [[e:stamford-lincolnshire|Stamford]] in 917 and 918. After a Norse revival from York, Edmund of [[e:england|England]] recovered the Five Boroughs in 942, an event celebrated in a poem in the [[e:anglo-saxon-chronicle|Anglo-Saxon Chronicle]]. The region kept distinct legal customs into the 11th century.
