free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.t: Small Catholic imperial city surrounded by Protestant Württemberg, best known as the birthplace of the astronomer Johannes Kepler.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.o: [[e:weil-der-stadt|Weil]] grew on the [[e:wurm-nagold|Würm]] west of [[e:stuttgart|Stuttgart]] and belonged to the [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]], whose estates in the area passed to the Empire on their fall. It was then treated as an imperial city, confirmed in the 1270s, around 1275, its name, Weil the City, distinguishing it from nearby villages.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.r: A council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] ruled this small town with its handful of villages. It lived from farming, crafts and markets. Surrounded entirely by the [[s:duchy-of-wurttemberg|Duchy of Württemberg]], it often quarrelled with its powerful neighbour and remained Catholic when Württemberg turned Protestant. The astronomer [[e:johannes-kepler|Johannes Kepler]] was born there in 1571. Much of the town was burned in 1648 near the end of [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-weil-der-stadt.e: Württemberg finally annexed the town in 1802, ending its long resistance to its neighbour. It is now a small town in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]], with a [[e:johannes-kepler|Kepler]] museum in the house where the astronomer was born.

frisii.t: Germanic people of the North Sea coast who lived on artificial mounds and defied Rome by force and by diplomacy.
frisii.o: The Frisii lived on the coastal marshes of the northern [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] between the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] and the Ems. To survive floods they built terps, artificial dwelling mounds raised over generations. They became tributaries of [[e:rome|Rome]] after the campaigns of [[e:nero-claudius-drusus|Drusus]] in 12 BCE.
frisii.r: They paid tribute in ox hides. Roman sources describe no kings but war leaders and envoys; in 58 CE [[e:verritus|Verritus]] and [[e:malorix|Malorix]] travelled to [[e:rome|Rome]] and boldly took seats among the senators at [[e:pompey|Pompey's]] [[e:theatre|Theatre]], winning [[e:nero|Nero's]] admiration.
frisii.e: In 28 CE they revolted against exactions, hanging tax collectors and defeating the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] at the [[e:battle-of-baduhenna-wood|Baduhenna wood]]. [[e:rome|Rome]] later abandoned control. In the 4th century rising seas left much of the coast nearly deserted, and the area was resettled, later forming the [[s:frisian-kingdom|Frisian Kingdom]].

fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.t: The Libyan Fezzan under Free French military administration after its capture by Leclerc's forces from Chad, until Libyan independence in 1951.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.o: In late 1942 and January 1943 [[s:free-france|Free French]] forces under [[e:philippe-leclerc-de-hauteclocque|Philippe Leclerc]] advanced from [[s:chad-french-colony|Chad (French colony)]] and took the [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] from [[s:italian-libya|Italian Libya]]. [[e:france|France]] administered it as a military territory together with the oasis of [[e:ghadames|Ghadames]], with [[e:sabha-libya|Sabha]] as its centre.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.r: French officers governed in cooperation with the Sayf al-Nasr family, whose leader [[e:ahmad-sayf-al-nasr|Ahmad Sayf al-Nasr]] acted as chief of the territory. Parts were administratively linked to [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]] and southern [[e:tunisia|Tunisia]]. [[e:france|France]] hoped to keep the region to secure links between its North and Central African colonies.
fezzan-ghadames-military-territory.e: The [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] decided in 1949 that [[e:libya|Libya]] should become independent. The [[s:sultanate-of-fezzan|Fezzan]] joined the federal [[s:kingdom-of-libya|Kingdom of Libya]] at independence in December 1951 as one of its three provinces, though French troops stayed until 1956.

felsina.t: The leading Etruscan city of the Po valley, on the site of Bologna, until the Boii Gauls took it in the 4th century BCE.
felsina.o: Felsina grew from the Villanovan villages around modern [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]], the area that gave the Villanovan culture its name, from the 9th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE it became a city at the centre of an Etruscan expansion north of the [[e:apennines|Apennines]]; Pliny called it the chief of [[e:etruria|Etruria's]] cities in the region.
felsina.r: Felsina controlled farmland in the Po plain and the passes over the [[e:apennines|Apennines]] to [[e:etruria|Etruria]], and traded with the [[s:ancient-veneti|Veneti]], the [[e:celts|Celts]] and the Greek port of [[e:spina|Spina]]. Its cemeteries, such as the Certosa, contain the bronze [[e:certosa-situla|Certosa situla]] and horseshoe-shaped stone grave stelae carved with journeys to the afterlife. Little is known of its government.
felsina.e: Celtic [[s:boii|Boii]] overran Felsina around the mid-4th century BCE, and the town became [[e:bologna|Bononia]]. [[e:rome|Rome]] conquered the Boii and founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Bononia in 189 BCE, from which modern [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]] descends.

french-somaliland.t: France's colony on the Gulf of Aden around the port of Djibouti, the sea outlet of Ethiopia through its famous railway.
french-somaliland.o: In 1896 [[e:france|France]] combined [[s:obock|Obock]] and its [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] over the [[s:sultanate-of-tadjoura|Sultanate of Tadjoura]] and the [[e:issa-clan|Issa Somali]] coast into the colony of the Cote francaise des [[e:somalis|Somalis]], with its capital at the new port of [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]], founded by [[e:leonce-lagarde|Leonce Lagarde]]. The borders were fixed by agreements with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]].
french-somaliland.r: The colony lived on its port and on the [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]] to [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]] railway, completed in 1917, which carried most of [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia's]] foreign trade. Its population of [[e:afar|Afar]] and [[e:issa-clan|Issa Somali]] pastoralists, Arab traders and French officials was small. During the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] it sided with Vichy until British [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]] forced it to join [[s:free-france|Free France]] in 1942.
french-somaliland.e: In referendums in 1958 and 1967 voters chose to remain French, amid protests and charges of manipulation. In 1967 the colony was renamed the [[s:french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-issas|French Territory of the Afars and the Issas]].

free-imperial-city-of-goslar.t: Harz imperial city of the Salian emperors' palace and the Rammelsberg silver mine, whose wealth made it a leading Hanseatic town.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.o: [[e:silver|Silver]] was found in the [[e:rammelsberg|Rammelsberg]] near Goslar in the 10th century, and the Salian emperors built an imperial palace there, where [[e:henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor|Henry III]] often resided. The town grew rich from mining and metal trade. After the decline of royal power it gradually took control of its own affairs and was a free imperial city by around 1290.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.r: A council dominated by mine owners and merchants ruled. [[e:silver|Silver]], [[e:copper|copper]] and lead from the [[e:rammelsberg|Rammelsberg]] brought Goslar great wealth, and it joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]]. The city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1528. In the [[e:treaty-of-riechenberg|Treaty of Riechenberg]] of 1552 it lost control of the mine and forests to [[e:henry-v-duke-of-brunswick-luneburg|Henry the Younger]] of the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]], beginning a long decline.
free-imperial-city-of-goslar.e: Goslar lost its freedom in 1802 to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], belonged to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] from 1807 and to the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]] from 1816. Its old town and the [[e:rammelsberg|Rammelsberg]] mine are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.t: One of the smallest imperial cities of the Empire, a Swabian market town at the foot of the Ipf, a celebrated Celtic hillfort.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.o: Bopfingen lies beneath the Ipf, a hill crowned by a major Celtic princely seat of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. The medieval town grew under the [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] and appears among the imperial cities in the imperial tax list of 1241.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.r: Bopfingen was a modest market town with a tiny territory, governed by a council of [[e:burghers|burghers]] and dependent on its larger neighbour [[s:free-imperial-city-of-nordlingen|Nördlingen]] and on the Swabian city leagues. Its economy rested on farming, crafts and the local market. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 16th century and suffered heavily in [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-bopfingen.e: Bopfingen lost its freedom in 1802, passing first to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]] and in 1810 to the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. It is now a small town in [[e:baden-wurttemberg|Baden-Württemberg]], and the Ipf is a protected archaeological site.

ferozepur-state.t: A Sikh chiefship on the Sutlej whose lapse to the British in 1835 gave them a forward base against the Sikh kingdom of Lahore.
ferozepur-state.o: After the fall of Mughal [[e:sirhind|Sirhind]] in 1763–64 a [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] sardar took [[e:firozpur|Ferozepur]], an old town on the south bank of the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]].
ferozepur-state.r: [[e:firozpur|Ferozepur]] came under British protection in 1809 as one of the [[e:cis-sutlej-states|Cis-Sutlej states]]. For much of the period it was governed by a widow of the ruling family. Little detail of its administration is recorded.
ferozepur-state.e: When the line ended in 1835 the British took [[e:firozpur|Ferozepur]] and turned it into a cantonment facing the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] across the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]]. It served as the main base for the Anglo-[[e:sikhism|Sikh]] wars and remains a district town of Indian [[e:punjab|Punjab]].

free-state-of-coburg.t: Brief Franconian republic that, after a 1919 referendum, chose to join Bavaria rather than Thuringia.
free-state-of-coburg.o: Duke [[e:charles-edward-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha|Charles Edward of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha]] abdicated in November 1918. [[e:coburg|Coburg]] and [[e:gotha|Gotha]], legally separate since 1826, went their own ways: Gotha joined [[e:thuringia|Thuringia]], while Coburg became a free state of its own, with its parliament meeting in Coburg.
free-state-of-coburg.r: The free state existed only briefly and had few powers beyond managing the transition. Its main question was its future: too small to survive alone, it had to choose between the new Thuringian state and [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]]. In a referendum on 30 November 1919, about 88 per cent of voters chose Bavaria, partly because of [[e:coburg|Coburg's]] Franconian ties and Bavaria's favourable terms.
free-state-of-coburg.e: Under a state treaty [[e:coburg|Coburg]] joined the [[s:free-state-of-bavaria|Free State of Bavaria]] on 1 July 1920, keeping certain guarantees for its institutions.

free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.t: Allgäu imperial city on the Wertach, a linen-weaving town shared by Catholics and Protestants after the Thirty Years War.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.o: Kaufbeuren grew around a royal court on the [[e:wertach|Wertach]] under the [[e:house-of-welf|Guelphs]] and [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]], on the road from [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] into the [[e:alps|Alps]]. After the fall of the Hohenstaufen it was recognised as an imperial city by Rudolf I in 1286.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.r: A council of patricians and [[e:guild|guilds]] governed. Linen and fustian weaving were the main trades. The city adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], but after 1648 Catholics and [[e:lutheranism|Lutherans]] shared its offices under the parity rules of the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]]. The Franciscan nun [[e:crescentia-of-kaufbeuren|Crescentia of Kaufbeuren]], later canonised, lived there in the 18th century.
free-imperial-city-of-kaufbeuren.e: Kaufbeuren lost its freedom in 1802 to [[e:bavaria|Bavaria]]. After the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] German refugees from [[e:jablonec-nad-nisou|Gablonz]] in [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] settled its suburb of [[e:neugablonz|Neugablonz]], bringing their glass and jewellery industry. It remains a town in Bavaria.

fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A line of Delta kings of largely Canaanite descent who ruled the eastern Nile Delta as the Middle Kingdom weakened.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: As the Thirteenth Dynasty lost its grip, around 1725 BCE a separate line of kings established itself in the eastern Delta, probably at [[e:avaris|Avaris]] (Tell el-Dab'a), where a large population of Levantine origin had settled. [[e:manetho|Manetho]] placed the dynasty at [[e:xois|Xois]] in the western Delta, but most scholars now locate it at Avaris.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Very little is known. The best-attested king, [[e:nehesy|Nehesy]], whose name means 'the Nubian', left monuments at [[e:avaris|Avaris]] and [[e:tell-el-muqdam|Tell el-Muqdam]] and honoured [[e:seth|Seth]] as lord of Avaris. Scarabs with royal names suggest a series of short reigns. The dynasty controlled the Delta's trade with the [[e:levant|Levant]], and its population buried their dead in Canaanite fashion, with donkeys and bronze weapons.
fourteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: The kingdom seems to have been weakened by famine and plague, and around 1650 BCE it was replaced by the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] rulers of the Fifteenth Dynasty of [[e:egypt|Egypt]], who also made [[e:avaris|Avaris]] their capital.

french-louisiana.t: France's colony in the Mississippi basin, founded around the Gulf coast and New Orleans, whose Creole culture still marks the state of Louisiana.
french-louisiana.o: In 1682 [[e:rene-robert-cavelier-sieur-de-la-salle|René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle]] travelled down the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] and claimed its basin for [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]], naming it [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]]. Settlement began when [[e:pierre-le-moyne-diberville|Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville]] built [[e:fort-maurepas|Fort Maurepas]] at [[e:biloxi|Biloxi]] in 1699. Mobile followed in 1702, and in 1718 his brother [[e:jean-baptiste-le-moyne-de-bienville|Bienville]] founded [[e:new-orleans|New Orleans]], the capital from 1722.
french-louisiana.r: [[e:john-law|John Law's]] [[e:mississippi-company|Company of the Indies]] ran the colony from 1717 to 1731, promoting settlement in a speculative boom that collapsed in 1720. Thousands of enslaved Africans were brought, mostly from [[e:senegambia|Senegambia]], and the [[e:code-noir|Code Noir]] of 1724 governed [[e:slavery|slavery]]. [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]] stretched in claim to the [[e:illinois-country|Illinois Country]] and depended on Native alliances, though wars with the [[s:natchez-chiefdom|Natchez chiefdom]] and the [[s:chickasaw-nation|Chickasaw Nation]] were costly. It became a crown colony in 1731.
french-louisiana.e: Facing defeat in the [[e:seven-years-war|Seven Years War]], [[e:france|France]] secretly ceded [[e:new-orleans|New Orleans]] and the land west of the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] to [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1762, creating [[s:spanish-louisiana|Spanish Louisiana]], while the eastern lands went to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1763.

free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.t: The guild-run republic on the Rhine where Gutenberg experimented with printing and Martin Bucer led the Reformation, before Louis XIV annexed it in 1681.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.o: The [[e:burghers|burghers]] of Strasbourg had long resented the rule of their [[e:bishop|bishops]]. In 1262 they defeated [[e:walter-of-geroldseck|Bishop Walter of Geroldseck]] at the battle of [[e:battle-of-hausbergen|Hausbergen]] and won self-government, and the city soon became a free city of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], outside the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg|Prince-Bishopric of Strasbourg]].
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.r: From 1332 the [[e:guild|guilds]] shared power with the patricians in a council and magistracy. Strasbourg traded along the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], finished its cathedral spire in 1439, and hosted [[e:johannes-gutenberg|Johannes Gutenberg's]] early work. It adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1520s under [[e:martin-bucer|Martin Bucer]], while [[e:jacob-sturm|Jacob Sturm]] led its diplomacy and [[e:johannes-sturm|Johannes Sturm]] founded its [[e:gymnasium|Gymnasium]]. The first printed newspaper appeared there in 1605.
free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg.e: In 1681, during peacetime, [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV's]] troops surrounded Strasbourg and forced it to surrender. It kept its Lutheran churches and local institutions, but became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], confirmed by the [[e:treaty-of-ryswick|Treaty of Ryswick]] in 1697.

french-ivory-coast.t: The French colony on the Gulf of Guinea that became the leading coffee and cocoa producer of French West Africa and independent Ivory Coast in 1960.
french-ivory-coast.o: [[e:france|France]] signed treaties at [[e:grand-bassam|Grand-Bassam]] and [[e:assinie|Assinie]] in 1843, and merchants such as [[e:arthur-verdier|Arthur Verdier]] kept a French presence. In 1887-1889 the explorer [[e:louis-gustave-binger|Louis-Gustave Binger]] secured treaties in the interior, and in 1893 the [[e:ivory-coast|Ivory Coast]] became a colony with Binger as governor. The capital moved from Grand-Bassam to [[e:bingerville|Bingerville]] in 1900 and to [[e:abidjan|Abidjan]] in 1934.
french-ivory-coast.r: Conquest of the forest peoples was slow and violent, culminating in Governor [[e:gabriel-angoulvant|Gabriel Angoulvant's]] campaigns of 1908-1915. The colony, part of [[s:french-west-africa|French West Africa]], exported [[e:timber|timber]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and cocoa, grown on European plantations and increasingly by African farmers using migrant labour from [[s:french-upper-volta|French Upper Volta]]. Forced labour favoured European planters until the [[e:african-agricultural-union|African Agricultural Union]] of [[e:felix-houphouet-boigny|Felix Houphouet-Boigny]], founded in 1944, campaigned against it; it was abolished in 1946.
french-ivory-coast.e: [[e:felix-houphouet-boigny|Houphouet-Boigny]], who also served as a minister in [[e:paris|Paris]], led the territory to autonomy within the [[e:french-community|French Community]] in 1958 and to independence on 7 August 1960. He remained president until his death in 1993, and [[e:abidjan|Abidjan]] grew into a major West African metropolis.

first-mexican-republic.t: Mexico's first federal republic, created by the Constitution of 1824 and torn by coups between liberals, conservatives and Santa Anna.
first-mexican-republic.o: After the fall of the [[s:first-mexican-empire|First Mexican Empire]], a constituent congress adopted the federal Constitution of 4 October 1824, modelled partly on the [[s:united-states|United States]] and the Spanish constitution of 1812. It created the [[s:second-federal-republic-of-mexico|United Mexican States]], with nineteen states and four territories, and [[e:guadalupe-victoria|Guadalupe Victoria]], a hero of the independence war, became the first president.
first-mexican-republic.r: [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] remained the sole permitted religion, and the army and church kept their legal privileges. Politics was dominated by rival Masonic lodges and military revolts: only [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]] completed his term. [[e:vicente-guerrero|Vicente Guerrero]] abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]] in 1829, the year [[e:antonio-lopez-de-santa-anna|Santa Anna]] defeated a Spanish reconquest attempt at [[e:tampico|Tampico]]. [[e:valentin-gomez-farias|Valentín Gómez Farías]] launched anticlerical reforms in 1833, and the treasury depended on customs revenue and foreign loans.
first-mexican-republic.e: [[e:antonio-lopez-de-santa-anna|Antonio López de Santa Anna]] turned against the reformers in 1834, and in 1835 a conservative congress replaced the federal system with centralist laws, the [[e:siete-leyes|Siete Leyes]], creating the [[s:centralist-republic-of-mexico|Centralist Republic of Mexico]]. The change helped provoke the [[e:texas-revolution|Texas Revolution]].

free-imperial-city-of-giengen.t: A small Swabian imperial city on the Brenz, later known worldwide as the home of the Steiff teddy bear.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.o: [[e:giengen-an-der-brenz|Giengen]] grew on the river [[e:brenz-river|Brenz]] in eastern [[e:swabia-bavaria|Swabia]] as a [[e:hohenstaufen|Hohenstaufen]] royal town. After a period in which it was pledged to the counts of [[s:county-of-helfenstein|Helfenstein]], the townspeople secured their freedom, and by 1391 Giengen was recognised as a free imperial city answerable only to the emperor.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.r: A council governed the small town and its few villages. [[e:giengen-an-der-brenz|Giengen]] lived from crafts, linen and the market for the surrounding farms, and it adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Lutheran Reformation]] in the 16th century. Its position near the [[e:danube|Danube]] exposed it to war, and in 1634, during [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years' War, it was almost completely burned.
free-imperial-city-of-giengen.e: In 1802 [[e:giengen-an-der-brenz|Giengen]] was annexed by Württemberg, becoming part of the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]] in 1806. In 1880 [[e:margarete-steiff|Margarete Steiff]] founded her toy business there, and Giengen an der [[e:brenz-river|Brenz]] remains the home of the [[e:steiff|Steiff]] company.
